utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Sterc, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sterc.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As part of your job as assistant minister for reconstruction and development, were you familiar with issues concerning the peaceful transition of Eastern Slavonia to Croatian government control, between 1996 and 1998?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, were you aware of the refugee issues concerning the -- both of return of Croat refugees to Eastern Slavonia and the situation concerning Serb civilians and Serb refugees in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And within the two-year mandate of UNTAES, were you familiar with what happened with Serbs living in Eastern Slavonia as that region was being transitioned to Croatian rule?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of that population left Eastern Slavonia and moved to Serbia. In fact, this migration of theirs was permanent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know of the Serb civilian population of Eastern Slavonia which was domiciled in Eastern Slavonia in 1991, do you know what percentage left Eastern Slavonia between 1996 and 1998, of the domiciled Serb population of Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part of the population is also included, but I -- I can't remember the figure right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me show you, Mr. Sterc, Exhibit D419.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go, please, to page 6 in the English, please. I think there's only an English copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if you look at paragraph 23, this is now -- just for the record, an OSCE report dated 8 September 1998. And it says that: "UNHCR estimates that between August 1996 and July 1998, some 16.000 of the 67.000 Serbs who were residents of the region before the war have left the country - mostly to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?" Now, that works out to a little bit more than 25 per cent of this domiciled Serb population left Eastern Slavonia. My question to you is, as an assistant minister responsible for issues of refugees and returns, did you have a -- an understanding as to what was causing 16.000 people to leave under a UN mandate from Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just if the question could be clarified. I'm not sure they left under a UN mandate. If --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, I -- in other words, they left while Eastern Slavonia was under UN administrative control. So if you understand the question, could you tell us why 16.000 domiciled people left Croatia for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or what was your understanding of why they left.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What was your understanding of the causes of why 16.000 people would leave for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia even though the territory was under UN administration?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer like this. I think that regardless of the administration of UNTAES in Podunavlje region, there was political and economic uncertainty there, and I think that was the main reason. I can only give you a comparison. From our information, at the time of the UNTAES administration in Podunavlje, about 900 non-Serbs were killed. And at the Working Group meetings, I always raised that issue. I always asked the question: What exactly happened in Podunavlje when Croatia did not have control of it? The migration of people from such areas is always something to be expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, we easily agree on that 16.000 out of 67.000 is a little bit less than 25 per cent than a little bit more, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me do the math in my head, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Four times 16 is 64, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Ms. Gustafson, you want to add to the math exam? No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd just like to point out that I believe that UNTAES mandate ended in January of 1998. This report is dated September 1998, so I'm not sure the question -- and the statistics are people leaving between August 1996 and July 1998, so I'm not sure the question about people leaving under the -- while the territory was under UN administration is entirely accurate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could ask the witness whether the UNTAES --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Its actually the mandate ended February 1998, Mr. President, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: February 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- if it makes a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Does that point of the Prosecutor make any difference in your answer, Mr. Sterc?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None. That changes nothing. Because that's the situation that prevailed and the migration of people from the eastern territories to Yugoslavia was not in dispute. This was a continuing process, regardless of the dates you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, can I add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this was a period from August 1996, around 18.000 people in our estimate left the formerly occupied areas and were given accomodation in Podunavlje. So very probably these figures here could be a little different in actual fact, and we got confirmation of that later when we started recording the population in Podunavlje. We got information that, in a certain period, 138.000 ID papers were issued in formerly UNTAES areas, issued mainly by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Sterc, I want to turn your attention to -- starting at paragraph 9.1 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And with the assistance of the usher, if I could give a hard copy of the statement to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has heard a lot about the Law on Temporary Takeover, and I'm not going to go through in detail with you other than what's in the statement. However, are you familiar with the fact that a -- sorry. You talk about in paragraph 9.1 the establishment of an agency so that a person had -- could sell their property to an agency of the Croatian government. And I'd like to turn your attention now to a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, this is 1D -- 65 ter 1D1561, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, this is -- I'm going to show you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could go to -- there are no pages numbers at the bottom, so we'll have to use the 1D numbers on the bottom right-hand corner, and it is at page 1D7161.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If it assists, I think it might be at the 56th page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Page 52 in the Croatian version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sterc, do you recognise this as the decree that established the agency for mediation in transactions of specified real estate?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you see that the decree is dated 24 April 1997. Is this the decree that regulated or established the agency which was able to then buy property from Serbs who wished to sell their property, rather than to return to that property in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's fortunate that you looking at the same time at the previous document dated 23rd April which concerns operative procedures and the next one is the document establishing this agency, which means that we had agreed much earlier, the Working Group, and when we agreed that in principle we need to embark upon the concept of return of all to their homes, we put forward the proposal to establish agencies in all the countries from which refugees and displaced persons needed to come from. So such an agency was established in Croatia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for the record the entire document on the screen is actually -- these are annexes to a report submitted by the Croatian government to the Croatian parliament in 1998, which concerns the programme that was passed in June of 1998 of the Croatian government on the return of refugees. When we get to that topic in my direct examination, I will be tendering the report and the annexes, because the actual programme is already admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn, for example, in this document to page -- to the next page and go to Article 3, which I think is still the same page in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It actually -- I'm interested in subpart 2, so if we could turn the page in Croatian as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "APN is authorised to purchase specified real estate in its own name and on the account of the Republic of Croatia. APN is authorised to assign this real estate to citizens of the Republic of Croatia." Article 4 says: "Specified real estate is considered as real estate which, according to the Law on Temporary Takeover and administration of specified property ... is placed under temporary administration of the Republic of Croatia." Now, this agency or colloquially referred to by the Working Group as the land bank is -- do you know if that's still in effect today? Does it still exist?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we turn our attention, in your statement you make reference to an agreement of the Joint Working Group on the operational procedures of return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, this is 65 ter 1D1555. I'm sorry, 65 ter 1D1556.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe this is referenced at paragraph 13 of your statement. Now, in your statement, you make reference to the fact that this was agreement of the Joint Working Group where the general principles of return had been established ... the exact words. I'm sorry, that it was a guiding document on return. And can you explain to us what you meant when you said this was a guiding document on return?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We wanted after long talks at the Working Group to sign a document and make it public to define only the basic procedures for return in order to show that, in Croatia, the issue of the return of refugees and displaced person, including Serbs, has really been moved from the field of politics to the field of humanitarian issues. In Osijek, all representatives of the international communities were present, as well as representatives of the Serbs and general satisfaction was felt when the document was made public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can please go to the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, we see the signatures of the person who is signed this document. This agreement, was it with members of the international community and obviously it was, but why with the UNHCR and UNTAES?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know how they chose the signatories within the various groups of the Working Group. Eduardo Arboleda was chief of the commission of the UNHCR in Croatia, and somebody was standing in for Mr. Fischer on behalf of UNTAES. But since all was agreed within the Working Group, I don't think it mattered much who would sign on behalf of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If you look through the document, the focus appears to be often Eastern Slavonia. And my question to you is, although the document deals with Eastern Slavonia, how does it relate, otherwise relate to returns in other formerly occupied parts of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just one of the steps we made to deal with the whole situation in order to implement our design of the return of everyone to their homes. The role of the UNTAES was particularly important, because they had an administration that was prepared to accept the principle under discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UNTAES administration, on behalf of the international community, was frequently a vehicle of new initiatives and even the previous document that we discussed, and I had forgotten to say that, related to the establishment of that agency, the first draft was brought to the Working Group by a representative of the UNTAES. I would like to especially emphasise the following. When this decree on the agency was made public, you should know that part of the public opinion thought that Croatia had just established an agency for ethnic cleansing. Of course, all of us were indignant because the entire document from the first to last letter was completely harmonised and agreed with the international community and such agencies were also established in other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You anticipated my next question. If you look at the page on the screen and if we could go back one page in the Croatian. The last four paragraphs, which I think are the same as the document that we had seen before where you said that we could see the previous document as well. In here it says, for example, paragraph 2: "The Working Group welcomes the suggestion to create an agency for mediation in the traffic of real estate and a land bank database of property and owners under the auspices of the ministry for reconstruction and development." Based on what you've just said, was the establishment of the land bank or the agency something that was deemed a necessary part of the resolution of refugee issues?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Moreover, we all believed that the agency would provide logistics to the operational procedures. We had agreed in various documents that every country should set aside certain funds, based on estimates, to fund the agency to deal with property issues, and when such property becomes state properties -- state property, it would be placed at the disposal of -- of returnees and refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that exhibit 65 ter 1D1556 be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1609.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in the period after Operation Storm, and in the years that followed, were you familiar at all with any positions taken by the leadership of the RSK in exile on the issue of refugee returns?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am. We attended a joint conference on return in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And what was your understanding as to what positions were being taken by the leadership of the RSK in exile on the issue of refugee returns?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their representatives were very explicit at that meeting, which was attended also by the representatives of the international community, and their position was that a large part of them did not wish to return to Croatia, but they wanted compensation for the property they had left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this conference took place in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date. But there were all the representatives, and even ministers from Croatia, from Republika Srpska, and the political representatives of the Serbs from the occupied areas. I don't remember the exact date, but it was widely reported on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of the leaders from the formerly occupied areas who were present at the conference?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally spoke only with those who were in charge of issues related to the return of refugees and displaced persons, and one of the names I remember is Sime Djodan. He was the one who presented that position at the conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were there any positions taken by Mr. Djodan or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name is Djodan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: By him or anyone else about the issue of whether they -- they sought individual returns to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other people took different positions. One of the positions taken was to demand certain conditions for return to Croatia. That is, they wanted to return to Croatia on the condition that the authorities in Croatia changed. Some were in favour of individual returns, but that was overshadowed by certain misgivings and fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And were there any positions taken on whether there should be mass return of Serb civilians to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for mass return by Serb civilians who had left occupied areas, all of us took the position that mass return could not be organised in that way. Representatives of Croatia, the international community, and the Serbs all agreed on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to show the witness a document which I need to seek leave to add to the 65 ter list. This is document 65 ter 1D2778.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, any objections against it having been added to the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Madam Registrar, may I have 65 ter 1D2778, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And while we're pulling that up, Mr. Sterc, could you explain to the Chamber why you couldn't have mass returns, or why did you take the position that you couldn't have mass returns?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mass return could not be organised for a variety of reasons, and not only in Croatia but also elsewhere. The representatives of the international community told us that in similar situations there was never a mass return. The return had to be well planned, organised, safe, and it was necessary for certain conditions to be met, in order for the return to be possible, such as reconstruction, certain finances, organisation, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn -- this is a report from Banja Luka by the AIM organisation, and if we could turn to page 2 at the bottom in the English. And page 2, bottom paragraph, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is a statement purportedly by Mr. Milan Babic, and it quotes him as saying as follows: "I'm not in favour of individual solutions of the problem of return because it would mean" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you could turn the page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "... Croatisation of the Serb returnees which would jeopardise collective rights of the refugees and blur the problem of the Serb people in exile. I am in favour of collective return, collective security, and collective rights of the Serbs which implies resolution of their political status. Because the Serbs from Krajina - Dr. Babic continues - have the political right to the territory of the Krajina. If the committee of Borislav Mikelic approaches the problem of resolving the return of Serb refugees in this way, there will be no conflicts between us - Dr. Babic says, adding that the government of Krajina operates in exile and that a special commission was established within it to deal with the issues of the status and rights of the refugees, cooperation with various organisations and institutions, so why not Mikelic too." Now, were you familiar with such positions being taken by Dr. Babic or anyone else in the Serb leadership or in the special commission established by the government of Krajina in exile with relation to the issue of return of Serb returnees -- refugees?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never spoke to these persons, but we could read their statements in newspapers, and they were also conveyed to us by representatives of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And where were these types of statements conveyed to you by members of the international community? Where were you when they would relay these types of statements?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, at the time, assistant minister for reconstruction and development, if what is the position you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What I meant was, what was the context in which you were having conversations with the international community on that subject?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, this was in the context of our discussions which model of return we should apply. Given that individual returns have proven to be rather problematic, given the situation on the ground, we all knew that a collective return was almost impossible, so the only one left was a planned return, an organised return of everybody to their respective homes within the framework of the agreed documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender 1D2778 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will become Exhibit D1610.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1610 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Madam Registrar, if we could have again 65 ter 1D1561, please. And we will be going to page 1D71-7166.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think it's page 61 in the English, if that assists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 56 in the Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is a document dated 2 October 1997, and it is the programme of the government of the Republic of Croatia on the establishment of trust, accelerated return, and normalisation of living conditions in the war-affected regions of the Republic of Croatia. Were you familiar with this document as part of your job as assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And there is an introduction in the third paragraph, there's a whereas: "During the war emotional and inappropriate language was used in the private and public arena so as to generalise guilt and strengthen feelings of hate and division."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go down to the seventh paragraph. If we could turn the page in Croatian, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Whereas the government of the government of the Republic of Croatia strives to promote a way of life in which forgiveness, tolerance, co-existence, and equal rights of all its citizens are a foundation for progress and development." It talks about "many citizens who took part in the armed rebellion against the Republic of Croatia have sought and been granted Croatian documents and that they have by this act accepted all the rights and obligations which derive from Croatian citizenship, including respect for and defence of the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Croatia, and that they have accepted the Republic of Croatia as their homeland and have expressed the wish to be included in its political, economic and social life, and in that way, to contribute to its prosperity."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then there's: "Whereas the restoration of trust between all its citizenships is of vital interest for the development of the Republic of Croatia as a state and as a respected member of the international community of states. "Whereas it is unconstitutional to distinguish between the former parties in conflict on the basis of ethnicity as such, a distinction results in collective guilt and ignores individual responsibility for crimes, and also ignores the positive role of members of various ethnic groups during the hostilities."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then we can skip to "The government --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "The government of the Republic of Croatia thereby adopts a programme on establishment of trust, accelerated return, and normalisation of living conditions in the war affected regions of the Republic of Croatia." It outlines what the goals are at the bottom of that page, creation of general climate of tolerance and security; realisation of equality of all citizens within -- with regard to the state administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The establishment of trust between all citizens, et cetera. It says under organisation: "The government of the Republic of Croatia shall establish a national committee for monitoring the realisation of the programme. And there are fields of competence," and I won't go through them all. But it seems to be comprehensive, it identifies political, legal, administrative internal affairs, economic, social, cultural, educational, reconstruction, and return and the media, all areas of the programme. For example, if we -- we turn to the third page ahead, under point 6, media. "In view of the important place of the media in a democratic society, the government shall recommend that: The media will promote the equality of all citizens and the need to co-exist in tolerance as the only democratically acceptable way of life. "The media promote the rights of citizens which derive from the legal system of the Republic of Croatia. "The media promote an atmosphere of tolerance, co-existence, respect for human rights, and dialogue for the resolution of future excesses," et cetera. Can you explain, Mr. Sterc, what this programme was, why it came about, and what its objectives were?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After all the different documents, talks, negotiations, we all knew that, ultimately, the whole story had to end in a comprehensive programme of return. We needed to invest a lot of effort, a lot of time into developing such a programme. Often representatives of the international community did not really have confidence that these documents would ever be adopted although we continually repeated that this was our intention and our wish. After this, we started to have joint public addresses by representatives of the international community, representatives of the Croatian government, and representatives of Serbs from the occupied territories who left Croatia. As president of the Working Group, this is what I requested from the very beginning, because I knew that only by such public addresses we could induce some confidence in both sides. After the adoption of this programme, it seemed that everybody was relieved. I'm talking about the politicians now. Although, for those of us who worked on this, we knew that our job was only beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me take you -- as I indicated, Mr. Sterc, to the Trial Chamber, these are all annexes to the programme of 1998, so while the document is on the screen, let me just point out a few things and then move this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go, Madam Registrar, to numbered page 1D71-7173, please. At the very bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, attachment 6 to the programme that was passed in 1998 in June was an attachment called programme for accomodation of the users of property under temporary administration of the Republic of Croatia which must be returned for possession and use to the owner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page, please, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now written after the constitutional court of Croatia had struck certain portions of that law. And then there's a position of the government interpreting the law after the decision of the constitutional court. Do you recall that this government interpretation was an annex to the programme that was passed in June 1998?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Madam Registrar, if we could go to page 1D71-7154 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That should be page 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 49 in the Croatian, please. Sorry, 49 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, while that's coming up, let me just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: 46 in the Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the agreement of the Joint Working Group on the operational procedures of return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn the page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You are, of course, listed as a member of the Working Group. Under guiding principles, in paragraph 4 and 5, it talks about the establishment of this land bank. And then the next paragraph says: "The Croatian government, UNTAES, and UNHCR will seek international funding for the implementation of the described mechanisms as they are formed." Do you know whether in fact the land bank received international funding so that the homes of those Serbs that didn't wish to return could in fact be purchased by the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we asked international assistance and we asked to have a reconstruction conference on Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was any assistance ever received for the land bank?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender 65 ter 1D1561, which is the report of the Croatian government on the programme for the return of refugees as well as all of the annexes. And the actual programme itself was tendered earlier in this trial as Exhibit D428.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour. I just -- in order to avoid any future confusion, the attachment we just looked at, attachment 3, is the same document that was just admitted as D1609. But no objection, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But now have then -- we can vacate the previously admitted, or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think it's easier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would help --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's easier in following the transcript. Then the report of the Croatian government and the Programme for Return and all annexes together was already tendered, so we're now talking about the -- yes. Now, it was in evidence but without the annexes, and now we have a full set of these documents. Madam Registrar, that would be number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D1611, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1611 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Madam Registrar, can we have Exhibit D428 on the screen. And just so that the record is clear, D428 is the actual programme, D161 contains a report sent by the Croatian government to the parliament for purposes of discussion of the programme, D428, as well as all of the annexes that were ultimately part of D428.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, this is the Programme for Return and care of expelled persons, refugees, and displaced persons passed on 26th of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we turn the page and go to paragraph 5. Actually, I'm sorry, in the Croatian it should be the preamble paragraph 5. There are several renumberings, so if we could scroll up in the Croatian, please, and go back one page in the Croatian. There we go, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says that: "In regard to the above, the government has detailed the following programme in cooperation with UNHCR that has a leading role in solving regional refugees issues as well as with support of --" and in the English it was translated as "OECD." I believe if we look in the original, the acronym is OESS which is in fact the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So this programme, Mr. Sterc, was prepared in conjunction with UNHCR and OSCE; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This programme originally encompassed nearly 100 pages. I wrote it personally by hand and also in cooperation with my team, and that was the version that we put forward to the UNHCR and OSCE to get their approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And did they approve of the plan?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The whole point of this item 5 is as follows. Once we agreed on the principle, that everybody should return to their respective home, obviously for return of Croats to Bosnia-Herzegovina, to Kosovo and Macedonia we needed the assistance of the UNHCR, and this is why we underlined this in the item 5 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go into introductory remarks at paragraph 4, it says: "The government of the Republic of Croatia has appointed a commission which consists of ..." and then the first point is "assistant minister for development and restoration of the president of the commission." Who would that would have been?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn the page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At the end of the list of members of the commission, it says: "The commission's aim is to elaborate and monitor implementation of the programme in cooperation with UNHCR. The commission shall meet regularly twice a month or as circumstances require." And then point 5: "Commissions from the previous provision 4 shall propose to the government a co-chairman to directly deal with return issues and who shall, with representatives of the international community, commissions from Article 11, donators and non-governmental organisations, can assist this coordinating committee for the superintendence of return." After this programme was passed, was in fact a commission formed and did you in fact monitor implementation in conjunction with members of the international community?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did meet. We were in touch even more often than mentioned here in this item.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 14 of your statement you say this is the most important document of the Working Group. And it says: "The programme was implemented until today with some minor changes." Is this programme still in effect, as far as you know, in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You were a -- you later became an assistant minister of defence in the government of Prime Minister Racan. My question to you is, are aware of any significant change in the model or the programme of return of refugees that occurred with the transfer of power from President Tudjman's government to new Prime Minister Racan's government?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was transferred to the Ministry of Defence in the new government of the now late Mr. Racan, I did not deal with this issue anymore. However, many of my former associates remained in those jobs, and I kept in touch with them, and they all told me that the programme was still being implemented and that the process we had defined together was continuing in the same intensity, with the same tempo, in the same form. There were no radical changes. The process just continued in the same form in which it had started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Sterc, I wanted to give you an opportunity to talk about any personal experiences that you had in the field concerning the return of Serb refugees. Can you explain to the Court what your personal experiences were concerning this issue?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to you for this question, and I would very gladly, if I'm allowed, to present my personal views, because it was a period, and those were issues that were probably the most difficult in Croatia at the time. All of us who were engaged in this work almost had no rest. Our teams worked almost 16 hours a day. We toured localities, we dealt with conflicts that occurred on the ground, and I'd like to share with you one personal view concerning the -- the international community. I believed we were doing the same job, that we had to work jointly to resolve all the problems that occur on the ground, that the return of the Serbs is not the only and exclusive interest of our group, that we should appear together in public --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I got the impression that you wanted to know more about what we find at the end of paragraph 8 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, that apparently is not how the witness understood the question. In your statement, Mr. Sterc, you refer to that you personally went to the field with the police, et cetera. I think that that's the type of experience Mr. Misetic would like to know more about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What happened, where did you go, when did you go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was about to say that. Individual returns, within a relatively short time after the liberation of Croatia, caused great tensions on the ground. Because of those situations, of course, Croatia was exposed to international accusations. For instance, when one family returned to Banovina, and that return had been agreed between us and the international community, we could hardly expect that, at the same time, around the house of the returnees, around 500 to 600 protesters would appear, people who were protesting against the return of that family. Those were local Croats whose houses around had mostly been destroyed. Of course, we had to intervene with the help of the police to protect the family, and I personally spent 24 hours on-site. And that's how we worked to create the conditions for the return of refugees and displaced persons, breaking psychological barriers on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You said you spent 24 hours on the ground. Where was it? What village? What was the name of the family that returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I really don't know. I can't remember it was in Banovina. I can't tell you the exact name of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it's not a problem. It can be checked. It was widely reported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, was that the -- did you have similar experiences, that you went to a place where there was unrest in relation to the return of a family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I also went to meet with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm asking about similar events. First of all, when this happened, in the Banovina area, when was it, approximately? I'm not asking for a date but perhaps a month. What year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was mid-1996. It was summer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The other occasions, if there were any, where you personally went to observe what problems there were with the return of a person, or of a family, or of a small group of families, could you give us another example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. After that incident at Banovina, which I believe was in the summer of 1996, I asked members of the international community to come and visit such places together with me so that we sent -- send out a joint message to people on both sides. Among others, to those who caused such tensions. We went to a place called Kuruzari in Banovina towards the end of 1996, perhaps early 1997. According to international reports, one Serb family had been beaten up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, this mid-1996 experience in Banovina, do you know what finally happened to the family? Did they stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly what happened, but the international community, in fact a source from the international community, let me know that the family had to return to Serbia eventually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So do I have to understand it as that the protection was not effective, or were there other reasons why they returned to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we had decided to give maximum protection to that Serb family with all the police forces we had. However, it was too great a stress for them, and they had decided already to -- to go back and wait for some better time to return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, your earlier answer said I don't know exactly happened, but the international community informed you that they had to return to Serbia. Now, apparently from your testimony I do understand that you did know the reasons why they had to return, that is, the stress. Could you give us more details. How long did they stay there, how long did they get police protection, did they -- I mean, you apparently give us an idea about the reasons why, but could you tell us more details about under what circumstances the stress, as you said, was too much for them? How many police was involved in protecting them and for how long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I could see, because I personally spoke to the family and visited their home, they looked rather scared. Two or three policemen were on guard for 24 hours, and when the protesters dispersed, the UNHCR also joined in the efforts to resolve this problem, and we realised that within the whole picture of ensuring returns, guarding one family for 24 hours made no sense. We realised it was necessary that the problem of returns had to be discussed publicly and the solutions would then have to be translated on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if I read your statement, you say: "I personally went to the field with the police and safeguarded these first families returning." Whereas from your testimony, I understand that you personally went to the field and that you were finally not able to create a situation in which the family would stay, which is not exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We failed to create such conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but your statement says you safeguarded these first families returning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I asked some of these questions because the answers of the witness are of a rather abstract level; whereas, the Chamber, apart from knowing about plans, developments, reports, et cetera, is, of course, also interested in what the effect of those plans and efforts were. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Let me note that the incident you're referring to is two years before the plans or one to two years before the plans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the -- I see that. At the same time, the answer, as we find it in the statement, is of an abstract level. We safeguarded these first families, whereas, apparently the experience of this witness was that they were not able to provide such a situation which made it possible for them to stay. That's the risk of going on an abstract level rather than to stay with the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I intended to do that once he started talking about it, and I was actually going ask him many of the questions that you had asked him, particularly about how long the police had to guard that family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but perhaps you could ask that, because I did but we have no answer yet. Mr. Sterc, three policemen, how long did they stay at the house of this Serb family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were outside the house. They stayed for a week, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How long did the family stay after you had visited them until they decided to return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose they decided the return when they were no longer able to withstand the stress of the protection and the pressure from the neighbours, and that's when we learned of it from the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was how long. A week, a month --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A week. I answered that. A week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean -- so the police was there for one week, and then they decided to return. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I can clarify Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify, did the family leave, Mr. Sterc, because the police left.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course, not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I move on to a different topic, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to explore that then as well. How do you know that it was not the police that -- because you earlier said it made no sense to keep the police all time there. Tell us exactly what then happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We obviously did not understand each other. Police had orders to guard the family 24 hours a day, and the police was withdrawn only after the family decided to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did you learn about the decision of the family to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were informed by the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And was an additional effort made to convince them that it was worthwhile to trying stay or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. The UNHCR informed us -- in fact, kept us informed, as it was them who were in constant talks with the family. Our job was to talk to the neighbours, to assure them and convince them that returns were going to be a normal thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Once you received the message that the family wanted to return, what action did you take? Did you go back to the place, did you give instructions that there should be talks with the neighbours or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly. We estimated that the most important thing was to talk to the neighbours, so that, in the future, there would be no protest, when the UNHCR and the Croatian government make a decision on another return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said you estimated that the most important thing to do was. Now, what did you do was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We talked to the locals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally spoke to the locals the day after the protests started, and since these were people whom we -- the Ministry for reconstruction and development could not return to their homes, it took a lot of persuasion to convince them that their homes, too, would one day be reconstructed. It was our estimate that frequent visits, field visits by us and the UNHCR --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. My question was what you did after you received the message that the family had decided to leave. That was, from what I understand, one week after the police had guarded them. Now, in your answer, you're going back to the moment you went there. But that's not what I asked. I asked what you did, once you received the message -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I had not understood at first. We called in a meeting of the Working Group, and we put that issue on the agenda and discussed possible solutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are there minutes of the meeting of the Working Group in which we could find this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Working Group did keep minutes, but I have to be perfectly honest, I personally, when I wanted to check all this, I could not get a hold of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who keeps the minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The minutes were kept by an employee in my office at the ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there any reason why you had no -- couldn't get ahold of them? Did they tell you they couldn't find them, they do not exist anymore, or you are not entitled to have access to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Ministry of Reconstruction and Developments and particularly the department for -- my department, moved four times since I left. And, obviously, the documents were all mixed up in the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you ask access to the documents? Most recently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not recently. I think the beginning of the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Going back to the situation with this family who had decided that they could not stay any longer, what did you do for the family, apart from scheduling a meeting of the Working Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had agreed at the Working Group that we should apologise on behalf of the Croatian government to that family, and we did. And we offered them accommodation, in fact, housing, under some safer conditions. In that particular case, the offer of was rejected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any documentation of this offer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. All that was dealt with at Working Group meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the family, I take it, did not attend in Working Group meetings, or did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... how was this offer relayed to the family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a rule, we would pass it on to the UNHCR, and the UNHCR would then pass it on to the family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did that happen in this case as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection as what accommodation exactly was offered to the family? Where, what kind of accommodation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember exactly, but I think it was one of the state-owned apartments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the family, were they living -- their own house where they couldn't stay, was that a detached house, was it with some land around it; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was a family house with a garden around it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Misetic, I'm aware that I took some of your time. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: 15 minutes. 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15 minutes. Then we'll first have a break. Let me just check another administrative matter. One second, please, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just rising in anticipation. You said, We'll first have a break, so I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You thought it really was time to have the break. We will have a break and we will resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for the late start, but we considered it to be important to further discuss among ourselves the MFI'd documents, that's the 92 ter statement and the "Globus" article, in order to provide Ms. Gustafson with some guidance so that she would know where we stand, and the rulings of the Chamber will be given at the end of the examination-in-chief, Mr. Misetic. And if there -- then there would be any further need to put questions to the witness, we'll consider that. But I don't think that a lot will come as a surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President my only point was going to be that if there is a negative ruling, then we're prepared to call the witness back to give Ms. Gustafson some time at a later date, but I don't believe that the Prosecution was ever precluded from introducing a document into evidence [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- late disclosure to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there is actually no need to wait until the end of the examination-in-chief, so ... The Chamber will admit into evidence the -- let me just find it. We'll admit into evidence the 92 ter statement with the exception of paragraph 3, paragraph 5 partially, that is, 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.4 are excluded. 5.5 which say what the programme does mention, or, rather, does not mention. There's no obstacle to admit that. I don't know whether you would still seek that, Mr. Misetic, if 5.1 to 5.4 are not admitted. We leave that to you. So 5.5, 5.6, 5.7 can be admitted, if you consider that of any use when the heading of 5 and 5.1 to 5.4 are not admitted into evidence. 7 is excluded from the decision to admit the 92 ter statement. The "Globus" article is admitted into evidence, but the Chamber makes the following observation. The probative value of the "Globus" article is found primarily by this Chamber in the fact that the "Globus" article has apparently served as a basis for dealing with refugee and migration problems. In the non-admitted paragraph 7 of the 92 ter statement, reference is made to the "Globus" article. On the basis of the viva voce testimony, the Chamber considers that what was find -- what was found in paragraph 7 and what is reflecting, for a major part what is found in the "Globus" article, is expert opinion. So, therefore, admission of the "Globus" article, as I said before is primarily because the Chamber heard testimony that factually these data were used, as the witness described, and that the probative value is not to be found, as far as the accuracy of the data are concerned, because the figures in the article, as in the statement, are the result of scientific analysis, of which the sources are unclear and of which the methodology is not clear either. The Chamber emphasises that, of course, this probative value of an admitted piece of evidence is commented upon, as I just did on behalf of the Chamber, as matters stand now. Ms. Gustafson gives this guidance to you, as to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's very helpful. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, do you recall approximately how many Serbs had returned to what used to be called Sectors North and South in Croatia up to the publication of the "Globus" article in 1998?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, the reports and the discussions we had, I believe there were some 30.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Following up on the questioning of Judge Orie before the break, with respect to these 30.000 people, can you tell us, in terms of their security, what measures needed to be taken as a general matter. Obviously, different situations require different levels of security. But as a general matter, how did the Croatian government ensure that these people would be safe, up until 1998, these 30.000 people?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the event in Banovina that we discussed previously, the tensions slowly calmed down because we visited the field on a number of occasions and there were a number of interventions by the Croatian government, first of all, concerning the reconstruction of the infrastructure. And it was less and less required to protect the returnees, intensively. So more and more the possibility of individual returns appeared and there were more and more individual returnees, and obviously our intention was to register all of the returnees and we wished to have them return to the situation that was, to the largest extent possible, the same as the situation that was there prior to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: After that first incident which we discussed prior to the break, nevertheless, did there continue to be incidents involving returnees to the area?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. But in those situations, we reacted in the following manner. We visited the location all together. You probably remember that there was an incident in Kostajnica, and then even the American state secretary came to Kostajnica. And on the spot there we held a meeting of the Working Group because we believed that in this way we would bring down some of the psychological barriers to the return that did exit, and generally speaking within the Working Group we agreed that any incident registered by anybody in the field would be resolved in such a way that we would all visit the location and matter together and we would all together talk to the people who suffered during the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, these 30.000 returnees by 1998, were they people who had -- who were -- who were as of that date, 30.000 people who had permanent residence in Croatia, who had returned from Serbia or Bosnia-Herzegovina? I should say from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, these were people who had permanent residence in the Republic of Croatia before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What about after the war? When they came back, did they stay permanently in Croatia upon return?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a lot of mobility concerning these people. Formally they returned. We registered them as returnees, but they often would go back to Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia and from there back to Croatia, so I'd say that this was a rather mobile population at the time. However, both us and UNHCR registered their official return to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now in terms of mobility, as a general matter, were they moving -- what were the reasons that they were moving back and forth?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they primarily came back in order to maintain their property, in order to do some work on their houses, in their gardens, and it was our assumption that some of them had jobs in Bosnia or in Yugoslavia, and this is why they would return there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, are you familiar with any polling that was ever been done among Serb and Croat refugees and about their intentions to ever return to formerly occupied areas? I believe it's referenced in your statement, actually.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This is what we insisted on. We wanted the UNHCR to make this service concerning their positions on return and their wish, whether they wanted to return or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How often would -- well, let me ask you a different question. Were you familiar with any -- ever familiar with any OSCE surveys or polls conducted amongst Serb and Croat refugees?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they had a contract with the polling agency Pus [phoen] from Zagreb which actually carried out these polls on their behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And have you ever seen the results of that poll?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we considered that, and the results mostly confirmed our opinions and the discussions we had at the Working Group. So there were positions in a range from the -- that they did not want to come back to Croatia, to they wanted to come back to Croatia but under certain circumstances. So there was a wide range of answers, and generally speaking, those that were not willing to come back to Croatia wanted some compensation for their property, and those who were willing to come back, wanted the return to be organised and dignified with full protection by Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could have 65 ter 1D1151, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sterc, I'm going to show you a poll conducted in 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the use of this exhibit. It's a poll conducted in 2004, polling the -- surveying the emotional and motivational factors of Serbs regarding their desire to return to Croatia. First of all, it's polling those intentions, at the time the survey was taken in 2003. Secondly, it polls Serbs who left Croatia between 1990 and 1997. Only 47 per cent of the respondents left in connection with Operation Storm, and there is no way to distinguish their responses from the responses of the other respondents in the survey results. And so for these two reasons, in our submission, this report is irrelevant to motivations emotional factors regarding the desire of the Krajina Serbs to return to the Krajina after Operation Storm with respect to any reasonable time-frame after 1995. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that's an objection on admissibility -- oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was going say that I don't think there is an objection there actually as to putting the matter to the witness, a legal objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I objected on the basis of relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And the second point I was going to get to was first: There is no basis under Rule 89(D) to exclude it. Secondly it is relevant. The Prosecution's case is not that Croatia blocked Serbs from sectors north and south from returning but as a general policy of the joint criminal enterprise to prevent all Serbs and unless the Prosecution is saying that -- may I finish?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I'd just ask Mr. Misetic to be careful what he says about the Prosecution's case in front of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least it gives us as an impression of what Mr. Misetic thinks the Prosecution's case is. Ms. Gustafson, whenever Mr. Misetic or Mr. Kehoe or Ms. Higgins or Mr. Mikulicic is speaking about the Prosecution's case, the Chamber will always consider whether that is congruent with the content of the Prosecution's case, and the way in which the Prosecution interprets its case itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I fully understand that, Your Honour. My concern was that it was in the presence of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection -- the document can be put to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and once we've also seen it, because it's very difficult to talk about relevance if you haven't seen it yet, and we'll therefore consider whether it's -- finally its weight or admissibility which is at stake. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You can see, sir, this is from 2004, motivational and emotional factors regarding the return of refugees. It is correct that it not only includes Serbs but also includes the motivational factor for Croats to return. And if we go to the foreword, which is on page 4 in the e-court version. If we go to the third paragraph it says: "Since the process of return started in 1995, the Croatian government registered a total of 321.400 returnees. Two thirds of that number relate to ethnic Croats who were resettled within Croatia during the war. Approximately one third relates to Croatian Serbs who fled to Serbia and Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, or the Croatian Danube region in Eastern Slavonia." Now, 100 -- basically the numbers, if my math serves me well, 100.000 plus of these returnees are Serb returnees. And as of 2003, first, Mr. Sterc, and again you were at least a member of the Racan government at the relevant time-period. Are you aware of any other programme of return of these 100.000 Serb refugees other than the programme that you say you wrote by hand in 1998 under which they would have come back to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware -- yes, I was aware that that programme was being implemented. As I said, I don't participate in its implementation after the year 2000, but according to the reports that we received the report was still being implemented, and these numbers regarding the year 2003, if we go back to see the trends, this was a logical continuation of everything that was prepared in various other documents and in the programme itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I haven't heard an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But was there -- were you aware in 2003 of any other programme of return in force at that time, other than the programme that you had prepared by hand in 1998?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no other programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we move forward two pages, please, to page 6 in the e-court. Page 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the introduction in the third paragraph it describes the goal of this polling project: "The goal of this particular phase of the research segment of the project ... was to establish the basic motivational and emotional factors of return of Serb refugees to Croatia and the perception of the local Croatian population regarding their return."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go to page 11 in the e-court, which is a summary. Page 8 in the Croatian version, please. And just for the record, Mr. President, I believe the report indicates that it is an OSCE commissioned poll, and there's a stamp of the US agency for international development on there -- on the report itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Under war and war damages of the respondents, it says: "36 per cent of the Serb population left their homes in 1991, and 47 per cent of them during and immediately after Operation Storm in 1995. More than 50 per cent of them left Croatia in a massive collectively organised night, and as the main reason for the same they stated the inexistence of normal living conditions and fear." And if we go under life today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, may I ask you, this apparently is a -- this is a summary of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Entire report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are there questions -- of course, the Chamber hasn't seen it. Are there any questions about organisation of departure or is this opinion that slips in. That's again the problem if you haven't seen the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the questions are attached to the report, and number 8 says in what way did you leave Croatia and the options are: 1, in a massive escape together with other people from your place; 2, organised together with others but it was not an escape; 3, independently with my own family; and the last one is, does not know, refuses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which gives a -- or options, the one not exclusive from the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But -- we'll then have a closer look at it, but, of course, not having -- that's the problem with this system, where there's no way that you can go through every letter of a document which is understood by the Chamber and is well understood by the parties as well, but leaves us now and then in some fog. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just to clarify that I read that out from an English version we located on the web because it was only a partial translation of the first ten pages provided to us by the Gotovina Defence, so it is a slightly different document than the one on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just putting this, because it -- it -- it relates to a rather vital point of dispute in this case, isn't it, how organised and organised by whom the departure was. And I haven't seen the report, I'm not a statistical expert, but, of course, everyone knows that there are lies, big lies, and statistics, and not to disqualify this report, but well, to tell that you we should be very cautious in using this type of material. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's, of course, the case. However, in issues of trends and what people would have understood to be motivational factors at the time, I think it's relevant from that sense whether the percentages are plus or minus ten, isn't the point of what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the problem is usually in which way the questions are phrased and what options are given to the respondents to tick one of the boxes, whether these are really options which are overlapping options, or not. I mean, I think there might be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that and also that -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... please proceed, but just for you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm not talking about selection and where to find all the remaining Serb refugees who have not returned. But, again, this is -- this needs almost expert knowledge to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Apparently we have one on the stand, Judge, so ... I'm just kidding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just kidding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're just kidding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Under life today, it says: "41 per cent of Serb refugees from Croatia own a flat or a house in their current place of residence." It goes on: "In the future intend to build their own house or buy a flat in the current place of residence," et cetera? And if we turn a page under return. Under attitudes of returns: "Only approximately 14 per cent of Serb refugees from Croatia, to a certain degree, expressed an intention to return to Croatia, and only 4 per cent of the respondents from that group expressed a somewhat firm intention." And then the next paragraph concerns what the perceived major obstacles to return are. My question to you, Mr. Sterc, is, in terms of - and we don't need to discuss the specific numbers here - but in terms of what some of the factors were in terms of getting people to return how big of an issue was it, whether people wished to return?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN STERC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was exceptionally important, in order for us to be able to develop an operational plan of return at the Working Group, and this was the plan that we then submitted to the Croatian government and public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What -- in terms of you and the Working Group, what were your understandings of some reasons that people wouldn't want to return to Croatia ever? I'm not talking about the people in the short-term who had maybe security concerns, but of the people who decided that they wouldn't -- or didn't have a long-term plan to return to Croatia, what was your understanding of what some of those motivational factors were?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure its been established that there was such a group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me re-read the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. I'm afraid I did not fully understand your objection, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: My objection, Your Honour, is that it was a leading question because it hadn't been established from the witness that there was such a group and yet --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A Working Group --
